prediction_ref.short_label: Durable ask-user checkpoints become a standard harness primitive by H1 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Direct, strong continuation of the durable-execution thread this prediction lives in - and today supplies two same-day data points from opposite poles. OpenAI's acquisition of Ona (the rebranded Gitpod) folds into Codex a product that runs coding agents inside persistent cloud sandboxes, so a multi-hour or multi-day task keeps executing after the developer's workstation powers off and the developer reviews the run and gives feedback when they return - a durable, restart-surviving substrate with a human-review checkpoint built around it, explicitly framed as contesting the enterprise coding workflow. On the other side, Moonshot's Kimi Work ships an always-on local Agent Swarm (about 300 sub-agents) on the open-weight Kimi K2.6 that fires overnight jobs through a built-in cron engine with a keep-awake toggle and leaves the user's original files untouched unless changes are approved - a durable local runtime with an explicit human-approval gate. Both harden the same instinct the prediction names: long-horizon agent execution that survives the session, with an operator checkpoint to review or approve. The divergence from the exact marker is that neither ships the specific durable ask-user/checkpoint primitive as a named, generalized harness API - Ona's is review-on-return and Kimi's is an approval gate, not a documented resumable ask-user suspension point - so this is high-relevance reinforcement of the substrate trend rather than a clean hit on the standardized primitive.

Both ship session-surviving execution with an operator checkpoint, reinforcing the suspend-and-resume substrate.
bridge.remaining_gap: Neither exposes a named, documented resumable ask-user suspension point as a generalized harness API; both are bespoke review-on-return or approval gates, not the standardized primitive.

prediction_ref.short_label: Open agent harness powers a second vendor's first-party agent by Q4 2026

validation_rows.evidence_summary: The June 4 prediction tracks an open agent harness becoming the substrate beneath another vendor's shipped first-party agent. Today's Kimi Work is a concrete instance of the broader pattern: Moonshot shipped a first-party desktop agent product - an Agent Swarm coordinating about 300 parallel sub-agents driving the logged-in browser and firing cron jobs - running directly on its own open-weight model, Kimi K2.6 (open-weight Mixture-of-Experts, ~32B active per token, 256K context), with those same weights already runnable on-device through Unsloth's 2-bit dynamic quantization. That is a vendor building a packaged agentic product on top of openly published model weights and an open local-execution stack, which is the spirit of the prediction. The gap to the exact marker is that the open component here is the open-weight model, not a separately published open agent-harness framework that a second distinct vendor adopted - Kimi Work's swarm orchestration is Moonshot's own first-party harness, so it is supporting evidence for open-stack first-party agents rather than a clean second-vendor-adopts-an-open-harness hit.

A vendor packaging a branded agent atop an openly published stack matches the spirit, but the open piece is the model, and the orchestration is Moonshot's own harness, not an adopted one.
bridge.remaining_gap: No second distinct vendor adopted a separately published, tracked open agent-harness framework as its engine; the open component is the weights, and the swarm orchestration stays first-party.

prediction_ref.short_label: Compute-thesis IPO supply triggers measurable AI-equity crowding by Q4 2026

validation_rows.evidence_summary: The June 4 prediction watches large compute-thesis IPO supply clearing the market for a crowding tell. Today's corporate-activity story is squarely on the supply side of that mechanism: Anthropic confidentially filed a draft Form S-1 on June 1 (on a $65B round at a $965B post-money and a run-rate past $47B) setting up an IPO season against OpenAI, which is targeting at least $60B at up to a $1 trillion valuation and is expected to list by year's end, and the backdrop turned concrete when SpaceX priced 555.6 million shares at $135 to raise about $75B - the largest IPO in history, eclipsing Saudi Aramco - resetting the ceiling for how much capital public markets will absorb for one high-multiple name. That is exactly the IPO-supply build-up the prediction keys on. What is missing is the crowding readout itself: today's news carries the issuance and filing volume but no observed below-range print on the offering and no measured drawdown across already-public AI-infrastructure names as the supply clears, so the supply pipeline is densifying without yet supplying the measurable-crowding evidence the landing requires.
